Saying: God helps those who help themselves
WhatItMeans: People take it to mean God rewards self-reliance: His help goes to those who first get moving on their own, and waiting on God without acting is just laziness.
WhatTheBibleSays: Scripture says almost the opposite: "when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly" (Romans 5:6), and Paul learned that God's strength is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). The Bible does call for diligence, and trusting the Lord with all your heart (Proverbs 3:5) goes with working faithfully rather than sitting idle, but help comes because God is gracious, not because we earned it by helping ourselves first. I hold that the saying gets the order backwards: God helps the helpless, and then His help moves us to act.
Origin: The idea is ancient Greek, told in Aesop's fable of Hercules and the wagoner, where the god tells the stuck farmer to put his own shoulder to the wheel. The English wording first appears in Algernon Sidney's Discourses Concerning Government (1698) and was made famous by Benjamin Franklin in Poor Richard's Almanack (1736).
Sources: Aesop, Hercules and the Wagoner; Algernon Sidney, Discourses Concerning Government (1698); Benjamin Franklin, Poor Richard's Almanack (1736); on-site KJV text

Saying: Cleanliness is next to godliness
WhatItMeans: People take it to mean that being physically clean, washed, tidy and well-kept, is a mark of spiritual goodness, almost a spiritual duty in itself.
WhatTheBibleSays: The Bible cares deeply about purity, but it is purity of heart, not of hands: "Create in me a clean heart, O God" (Psalm 51:10), and Jesus taught that what defiles a person comes from within, not from unwashed hands (Mark 7:15). God did give Israel washing laws (Leviticus 11:44), yet those pointed to holiness, not to soap as a virtue. My position is that a tidy house is a fine thing, but it is not godliness, and treating it as such shames the poor and confuses outward appearance with a clean heart.
Origin: First recorded in John Wesley's sermon "On Dress" (1778), where Wesley quotes it as an existing saying, "Cleanliness is, indeed, next to godliness", so the phrase is older than Wesley, though its earlier source is not known.
Sources: John Wesley, sermon On Dress (1778); on-site KJV text

Saying: Money is the root of all evil
WhatItMeans: People take it to mean money itself is evil, so having it, or wanting it, is the source of every wrong in the world.
WhatTheBibleSays: Paul wrote something narrower and sharper: "the love of money is the root of all evil" (1 Timothy 6:10). One small word changes everything: the danger is loving money, not holding it. Jesus said no one can serve both God and mammon (Matthew 6:24), and Hebrews 13:5 tells believers to be content, yet Scripture also treats wealth as a tool to be stewarded and given generously. I believe the misquote does real harm: it lets greed hide behind a shrug at money itself, when the Bible's charge is aimed at the heart that trusts in riches.
Origin: A misquote of 1 Timothy 6:10. The popular form drops the word "love", turning Paul's warning about the love of money into a claim about money itself.
Sources: On-site KJV text, 1 Timothy 6:10

Saying: God won't give you more than you can handle
WhatItMeans: People take it as a promise that God caps every hardship at what they can bear, so no suffering will ever be more than they can cope with.
WhatTheBibleSays: The verse behind it, 1 Corinthians 10:13, is about temptation, not suffering: God "will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able" and makes a way of escape. About suffering Paul says the opposite: he and his companions were "pressed out of measure, above strength" (2 Corinthians 1:8), and it happened so they would trust God rather than themselves (2 Corinthians 1:9). I hold that the saying, meant as comfort, can wound: when life is genuinely more than someone can handle, it tells them God broke a promise He never made, instead of pointing them to the God who carries what we cannot.
Origin: A modern folk paraphrase that stretches 1 Corinthians 10:13, swapping "temptation" for suffering in general. No single author or date is known for the wording.
RelatedTopics: Temptation; Suffering; Hope in suffering; Endurance
Sources: On-site KJV text, 1 Corinthians 10:13; 2 Corinthians 1:8-9

Saying: This too shall pass
WhatItMeans: People take it to mean that no season lasts forever: hard times will end, and good times will too, so hold steady and do not cling too tightly to either.
WhatTheBibleSays: Scripture agrees that seasons change: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven" (Ecclesiastes 3:1), and Paul calls present affliction "but for a moment" beside eternal glory (2 Corinthians 4:17). But the Bible does not stop at impermanence: it anchors hope in what does not pass, God's word and His promises, which endure when everything else fades. My position is that the saying is true as far as it goes, but on its own it is only half a comfort; the full comfort is that the God who outlasts every season is holding us through it.
Origin: A Persian fable about a king who asks his wise men for a sentence true in every circumstance and receives a ring engraved with these words, told in the poetry of the 12th-century Sufi poets Sanai and Attar of Nishapur. It reached English through Edward FitzGerald's retelling in 1852 and Abraham Lincoln's speech at Milwaukee on 30 September 1859.
Sources: Attar of Nishapur, Ilahi-Nama (12th century); Edward FitzGerald, Polonius (1852); Abraham Lincoln, Address to the Wisconsin State Agricultural Society (30 September 1859); on-site KJV text

Saying: The Lord works in mysterious ways
WhatItMeans: People usually take it to mean that God has a hidden plan behind confusing or painful events, and that what looks senseless now will make sense in time.
WhatTheBibleSays: Scripture does teach that God's ways are beyond ours: "For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the LORD" (Isaiah 55:8), and Romans 11:33 calls His judgments unsearchable and His ways past finding out, while Psalm 77:19 says His footsteps are not known. But the Bible never promises that every mystery will be explained to us in this life; it calls us to trust His character when we cannot trace His hand. I believe the thought behind the line is sound, but the words themselves are a hymn writer's, not Scripture's.
Origin: William Cowper's hymn "God Moves in a Mysterious Way", written in 1773 under its original title "Light Shining out of Darkness" and first published in 1774 in John Newton's Twenty-six Letters on Religious Subjects.
RelatedTopics: God's Providence; God's Sovereignty; Trust; Suffering; Hope
Sources: Cowper, 'God Moves in a Mysterious Way' (written 1773, published 1774); on-site KJV text of Psalm 77:19, Isaiah 55:8-9 and Romans 11:33

Saying: To thine own self be true
WhatItMeans: People take it to mean that the highest loyalty is to your own nature and conscience — be authentic to yourself above all, and honesty to others will follow.
WhatTheBibleSays: No verse says this, and the Bible's counsel runs the other way: "Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding" (Proverbs 3:5), and "The integrity of the upright shall guide them" (Proverbs 11:3) — where the guide is uprightness before God, not the self. I hold that being true to yourself is only good counsel when the self you are being true to is shaped by God's truth, because the Bible never makes the self the final authority.
Origin: William Shakespeare's Hamlet, Act 1, Scene 3 (written around 1600-1601): Polonius's farewell advice to his son Laertes as he leaves for France — "This above all: to thine own self be true, And it must follow, as the night the day, Thou canst not then be false to any man."
Sources: Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act 1, Scene 3 (c. 1600-1601); on-site KJV text of Proverbs 3:5 and Proverbs 11:3

Saying: The lion shall lie down with the lamb
WhatItMeans: People picture it as a promise of God's coming peace, when natural enemies will rest side by side and nothing will hurt or destroy.
WhatTheBibleSays: The hope is real, but the pairing is wrong: Isaiah 11:6 says "The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid," and the lion in that passage eats straw like the ox (Isaiah 11:7), while Isaiah 65:25 repeats the wolf and the lamb feeding together. No verse anywhere pairs the lion lying down with the lamb. I believe the promise of peace is true, and I also believe in getting the words right — the lion and the lamb never lie down together in Scripture.
Origin: No single author — a centuries-old misquotation of Isaiah 11:6, repeated in preaching, art and hymns until it felt like Scripture. The earliest manuscripts, including the Septuagint, the Dead Sea Scrolls and the 1611 King James Bible, all read wolf, not lion.
Sources: On-site KJV text of Isaiah 11:6-7 and Isaiah 65:25; general discussion of the misquotation. No single source relied on or cited.

Saying: Love the sinner, hate the sin
WhatItMeans: It is usually taken to mean that you can love a person fully while condemning what they do, keeping the person and their sin separate.
WhatTheBibleSays: The Bible does command love of neighbour (Matthew 22:39), and it does call sin what it is: Jude 1:23 pictures rescuing people "hating even the garment spotted by the flesh," Romans 5:8 says God loved us while we were yet sinners, and Galatians 6:1 says to restore the fallen in a spirit of meekness. But Jesus never said this sentence, and it can be used to sound loving while judging. My position is that the sentence is a useful summary of something true, but it only works when the love is real and the speaker remembers their own sin first (Matthew 7:1-5).
Origin: St Augustine's Letter 211 (c. 424), written to a community of nuns: "Cum dilectione hominum et odio vitiorum" — "with love for mankind and hatred of sins." The modern English form was popularized by Mahatma Gandhi's autobiography (1929): "Hate the sin and not the sinner."
RelatedTopics: Love; Forgiveness; Sin; Judgment and mercy; Grace; Compassion
Sources: Augustine, Letter 211 (c. 424); Gandhi, Autobiography (1929); on-site KJV text of Matthew 22:39, Jude 1:23, Romans 5:8 and Galatians 6:1

Saying: When God closes a door, He opens a window
WhatItMeans: When one opportunity falls through, God has another one waiting just around the corner — a missed chance is never really a loss, because He always provides a better way in.
WhatTheBibleSays: Scripture does show God directing His people's steps — Proverbs 16:9 says a man's heart deviseth his way, but the LORD directeth his steps, and Acts 16:6-7 shows the Holy Ghost forbidding Paul from one place and redirecting him to another. But the Bible never promises that every closed door comes with an open window attached; Revelation 3:7 says Christ opens what no man can shut and shuts what no man can open, which is about His authority, not a guarantee of a painless Plan B. I believe God works all things together for good for them that love Him (Romans 8:28), yet my position is that a closed door sometimes simply stays closed, and trusting Him means accepting that, not expecting a window.
Origin: The line was made famous by the 1965 film The Sound of Music, where Maria repeats the Reverend Mother's saying, 'when the Lord closes a door, somewhere he opens a window.' Older versions of the door proverb, such as Alexander Graham Bell's 'when one door closes, another opens,' said nothing about God.
RelatedTopics: God's Providence; God's Sovereignty; Guidance; Waiting on God
Sources: Film dialogue, The Sound of Music (1965); on-site KJV text

Saying: Let go and let God
WhatItMeans: Stop struggling, stop trying to fix it yourself, and simply hand the whole thing over — if you let go completely, God will take over and carry it for you.
WhatTheBibleSays: Trust is commanded all through Scripture: Proverbs 3:5 tells us to trust in the LORD with all our heart and lean not on our own understanding, Psalm 46:10 says be still and know that I am God, and 1 Peter 5:7 tells us to cast all our care upon Him. But 'let go and let God' turns that trust into passivity, as if faith means doing nothing, while the Bible pairs trust with obedience and action — Philippians 4:6 tells us to pray rather than be anxious, and then to keep walking. I hold that the slogan gets the direction right and the method wrong: we do hand our burdens to God, but He never asks us to drop our hands from the work He has given us.
Origin: The slogan grew out of the Keswick Convention and the Higher Life movement of the late 1800s, which taught a crisis of full surrender as the secret of the Christian life; it later spread through recovery programs such as Alcoholics Anonymous and into Christian self-help. No single author can be credited with coining the exact words.
Sources: Keswick/Higher Life movement history; on-site KJV text

Saying: Idle hands are the devil's workshop
WhatItMeans: A person with nothing to do will drift into trouble — empty time is where temptation and mischief get their foothold.
WhatTheBibleSays: The Bible agrees that idleness breeds trouble: 2 Thessalonians 3:11 warns of some who walk disorderly, working not at all, but are busybodies, Proverbs 6:6 sends the sluggard to the ant to learn wisdom, and Proverbs 18:9 says the slothful in his work is brother to him that is a great waster. Proverbs 16:27 in the KJV does not say this at all — it speaks of an ungodly man digging up evil — though the 1971 Living Bible paraphrase rendered it as 'Idle hands are the devil's workshop.' I believe the warning itself is sound Scripture, but the saying is a proverb about it, not a verse from it.
Origin: The idea traces to St. Jerome, who wrote in the late fourth century, 'engage in some occupation, so that the devil may always find you busy,' and Geoffrey Chaucer repeated Jerome's advice in The Tale of Melibee, part of The Canterbury Tales, around 1386. The exact English wording is a later proverb, not a Bible quotation.
Sources: St. Jerome, Letter 125; Chaucer, The Canterbury Tales; on-site KJV text

Saying: The devil is in the details
WhatItMeans: A plan can look fine from a distance and still fall apart on the small print — the trouble hides in the particulars nobody bothered to check.
WhatTheBibleSays: This one has no verse behind it at all, not even a close one. Scripture does value care and diligence — Colossians 3:23 tells us to do whatever we do heartily, as to the Lord, Luke 14:28 tells us to count the cost before building, and Proverbs 21:5 says the thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness — but none of that is about a devil lurking in the fine print. I hold that the saying is sound practical advice dressed up in religious language, and it should be quoted as good sense, never as Scripture.
Origin: It is a twentieth-century inversion of the older German saying 'God is in the detail,' traced to a seminar given by art historian Aby Warburg in Hamburg in November 1925 and often wrongly attributed to the architect Ludwig Mies van der Rohe. The devil version first appears in print in the early 1960s and only became common in the 1990s.
Sources: German proverb history; on-site KJV text

Saying: Forgive and forget
WhatItMeans: Real forgiveness means wiping the offence from your memory entirely — if you still remember what someone did, you have not truly forgiven them.
WhatTheBibleSays: Forgiveness is commanded without question: Matthew 6:14 promises the Father's forgiveness to those who forgive men their trespasses, Ephesians 4:32 tells us to forgive one another as God in Christ forgave us, and Colossians 3:13 says the same. But forgetting is never commanded of us — the 'remembering no more' in Hebrews 8:12 is God's promise about His own forgiveness, not an order for ours, and 1 Corinthians 13:5 says love thinketh no evil, which is about not keeping a score, not about losing your memory. I hold that the saying confuses God's forgetting with ours: we are told to release the debt and refuse revenge, not to pretend the past never happened.
Origin: The phrase dates from the 1300s and was a proverb by the mid-1500s; a well-known early form is Cervantes' 'Let us forget and forgive injuries' in Don Quixote, and Shakespeare has 'Pray you now, forget and forgive' in King Lear. It comes from literature, not from Scripture.
Sources: English proverb, 14th century; Cervantes and Shakespeare usages; on-site KJV text

Saying: Don't judge a book by its cover
WhatItMeans: Don't decide what someone is worth, or whether something is good, from how it looks on the outside — appearances mislead, and the real value only shows on closer acquaintance.
WhatTheBibleSays: The Bible teaches the same caution in its own words: 1 Samuel 16:7 says man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart, and John 7:24 commands us to judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment. James 2:1 warns against having the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ with respect of persons. I believe the saying and the Scriptures agree here, but the proverb itself is not a Bible verse — it is a nineteenth-century saying that happens to point the same way the Bible does.
Origin: The exact wording appeared as a newspaper headline, 'Don't Judge a Book by its Cover,' in the Boston Daily Mail on 12 June 1849; a similar thought appears in George Eliot's The Mill on the Floss in 1860, where Mr. Tulliver concludes 'one mustn't judge by th' outside.' The sentiment is older, but the proverb is nineteenth-century, not biblical.
Sources: Boston Daily Mail headline, 12 June 1849; George Eliot, The Mill on the Floss (1860); on-site KJV text

Saying: Everything happens for a reason
WhatItMeans: People take it to mean that every event, even tragedy and evil, was planned by God for a purpose, so nothing is ever truly senseless.
WhatTheBibleSays: Romans 8:28 says God works all things together for good for those who love Him: He redeems what happens, which is not the same as saying He caused it or that it was good. Joseph told his brothers, "ye thought evil against me; but God meant it for good" (Genesis 50:20): their evil was real evil, and God bent it toward good. Jesus refused the same shortcut when a tower fell and killed eighteen people, saying they were no worse than anyone else (Luke 13:4). I believe the saying goes too far: it turns every wound into God's plan, when Scripture says God is sovereign over suffering without being the author of evil, and that He brings good out of what was never good.
Origin: A modern saying with no single known author. Early forms of the sentiment appear in 19th-century writing, George Borrow's Lavengro (1851) and Jules Verne (1874), and the exact modern wording appears in American magazines around 1916-1917. It is usually hung on Romans 8:28, which says something different.
RelatedTopics: God's Providence; God's Sovereignty; Suffering; Evil and Suffering; Faith and Reason
Sources: George Borrow, Lavengro (1851); on-site KJV text, Romans 8:28

Saying: Spare the rod, spoil the child
WhatItMeans: Most people who quote it mean that children who are not disciplined firmly will turn out spoiled, and that physical discipline is what the Bible prescribes.
WhatTheBibleSays: Proverbs 13:24 does say, "He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes," and Proverbs 22:15 and Proverbs 23:13-14 speak of correction in the same spirit, while Hebrews 12:6 says the Lord chastens those He loves. But a proverb is wisdom to weigh, not a command to strike, and the Bible's picture of discipline is loving, timely correction, never cruelty. My position is that the rhyme itself is not a verse, while the heart of it — loving discipline that does not leave a child to himself — is genuinely biblical.
Origin: Samuel Butler's satirical poem Hudibras, Part II (1664), where the line appears in a passage about lovers, not children: "Love is a boy by poets styl'd; Then spare the rod, and spoil the child." Butler was riffing on Proverbs 13:24, not quoting it.
Sources: Butler, Hudibras, Part II (1664); on-site KJV text of Proverbs 13:24, Proverbs 22:15, Proverbs 23:13-14 and Hebrews 12:6

Saying: God doesn't call the qualified, He qualifies the called
WhatItMeans: People take it to mean that God does not wait for the skilled, impressive or ready — He chooses ordinary, unlikely people and equips them for the work He gives them.
WhatTheBibleSays: The pattern runs all through Scripture: "God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise... and weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty" (1 Corinthians 1:27-28), Moses protested that he was slow of speech (Exodus 4:10) and God answered, "I will be with thy mouth" (Exodus 4:12), and Jeremiah said, "I cannot speak: for I am a child" (Jeremiah 1:6). I hold that the sentence is true to Scripture's pattern even though the words themselves are not a verse — God really does call the unlikely and then equip them.
Origin: No single known author — the wording is a modern saying, often credited to various preachers and writers (among them Mark Batterson's The Circle Maker), but no original source has been established, so its origin is honestly unknown.
RelatedTopics: Calling; Grace; Humility; Weakness; Faith; Discipleship
Sources: On-site KJV text of 1 Corinthians 1:26-29, Exodus 4:10-12 and Jeremiah 1:6-7; modern usage (e.g. Batterson, The Circle Maker). No single original source established.

Saying: Charity begins at home
WhatItMeans: Look after your own family and your own household first — your duty to those closest to you comes before giving time or money to strangers or outside causes.
WhatTheBibleSays: There is real Scripture behind the duty part: 1 Timothy 5:8 says that if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and Galatians 6:10 tells us to do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith. But the Bible never makes family the limit of generosity — 1 John 3:17-18 warns against shutting up our compassion toward a brother in need, and Matthew 22:39 commands love of neighbour as of self. My position is that the verse and the proverb overlap but are not the same thing: providing for your own is a duty, and using it as an excuse not to give beyond your own is not.
Origin: Sir Thomas Browne first printed the phrase in its modern form in Religio Medici in 1642 — 'Charity begins at home, is the voice of the world' — and he wrote it to argue against it, not to endorse it. The idea itself is older: Wycliffe expressed it in English in 1382, and the sentiment goes back further still.
Sources: Sir Thomas Browne, Religio Medici (1642); on-site KJV text

Saying: Pride comes before a fall
WhatItMeans: Someone who is proud and full of themselves is heading for a humiliating fall — arrogance always comes before the crash.
WhatTheBibleSays: The warning is thoroughly biblical: Proverbs 11:2 says when pride cometh, then cometh shame, Proverbs 18:12 says before destruction the heart of man is haughty, and James 4:6 says God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble. The problem is only the wording — Proverbs 16:18 in the KJV reads 'Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall,' so the popular saying stitches half of each clause together and drops 'destruction' altogether. I believe the saying is true, and my position is that it belongs on the borderline: close enough to the verse that a reader could fairly call it the verse in other words, yet not the verse itself.
Origin: It is a popular paraphrase of Proverbs 16:18, shortened over time until the two halves of the verse were folded into one line. No separate author or date stands behind it; it grew out of the verse itself as people repeated it from memory.
Sources: Proverbial paraphrase of Proverbs 16:18; on-site KJV text

Saying: To err is human, to forgive divine
WhatItMeans: Making mistakes is part of being human, the saying goes, and forgiving others is the godlike thing to do — so both halves sound like wisdom straight from Scripture.
WhatTheBibleSays: The two halves are true in their own way, but no verse puts them together. Romans 3:23 says all have sinned and come short of the glory of God, and Ephesians 4:32 tells us to forgive one another even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven us. The Bible never treats forgiveness as something divine in us, though — it treats it as something God does first, and then asks of us. I hold that the line is good poetry and sound counsel, but it is Alexander Pope's, not Paul's.
Origin: Alexander Pope, An Essay on Criticism, Part II, line 525 — written 1709, published in London in May 1711: "To Err is Humane; to Forgive, Divine." The shorter "to err is human" is older, a calque of the Latin errare humanum est, attributed to Seneca.
Sources: Alexander Pope, An Essay on Criticism (1711); on-site KJV text of Romans 3:23 and Ephesians 4:32

Saying: The road to hell is paved with good intentions
WhatItMeans: Good intentions on their own count for nothing — a person can mean well all the way to ruin, because meaning well is not the same as doing well.
WhatTheBibleSays: Proverbs 14:12 warns that "there is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death," and Jesus said the broad way leads to destruction (Matthew 7:13). James adds the other half: knowing good and not doing it is sin (James 4:17), and faith without works is dead (James 2:17). I believe the proverb's warning is thoroughly biblical — the Bible is full of people who meant well and still went wrong — but the sentence itself is an English proverb, not a verse.
Origin: A proverb with no single author and a disputed history. It is often attributed to Bernard of Clairvaux, but that attribution comes only from François de Sales writing in 1604, some 500 years later, and the line is not found in Bernard's works. Early English forms appear from the 1500s; John Wesley quoted "Hell is paved, saith one, with good intentions" in a 1741 sermon, and the full modern wording first appears in print in Henry G. Bohn's A Hand-book of Proverbs (1855).
Sources: John Wesley, sermon (1741); Henry G. Bohn, A Hand-book of Proverbs (1855); on-site KJV text of Proverbs 14:12, Matthew 7:13 and James 4:17

Saying: God said it, I believe it, that settles it
WhatItMeans: The speaker is declaring full confidence in Scripture — if God said it, that is the end of the argument, whatever anyone else thinks.
WhatTheBibleSays: God's word is indeed settled: "For ever, O LORD, thy word is settled in heaven" (Psalm 119:89), and all Scripture is given by inspiration of God (2 Timothy 3:16). But notice the order in the slogan — God said it, I believe it, that settles it — as if God's word waits on my belief to become settled. My position is that the slogan gets the order wrong: God's word is settled whether I believe it or not, and my belief is the response, not the seal. The sentiment is sound; the wording puts me in the middle where I do not belong.
Origin: No single author is documented. The phrase was popularised in the 1970s — the Heritage Singers published the song "God Said It, I Believe It" in 1975 and filmed a music video for it in 1976 — and it circulated widely as a bumper sticker. Billy Graham is sometimes associated with it, but there is no evidence he coined it.
Sources: Heritage Singers, "God Said It, I Believe It" (1975); on-site KJV text of Psalm 119:89 and 2 Timothy 3:16

Saying: Let your conscience be your guide
WhatItMeans: Your inner voice knows right from wrong, so the safest path through life is simply to follow what your conscience tells you.
WhatTheBibleSays: The Bible does speak of conscience — Romans 2:15 says the conscience bears witness, accusing or else excusing — but it never tells us to follow it as a guide, and for good reason: conscience can be misled. "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked" (Jeremiah 17:9), and Paul warns of consciences seared with a hot iron (1 Timothy 4:2). A clear conscience did not prove Paul right either — "I know nothing by myself; yet am I not hereby justified" (1 Corinthians 4:4). I hold that conscience is a witness, not a compass: it can tell you something is wrong, but only God's word can tell you what is right.
Origin: Best known from Walt Disney's Pinocchio (1940), where the Blue Fairy tells Pinocchio to "always let your conscience be your guide," and Jiminy Cricket sings it in "Give a Little Whistle." An older origin is sometimes claimed — Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab is said to have used the words in his address at Jabiah after the surrender of Jerusalem (c. 638) — but no primary source verifies the English wording as an accurate translation, so that attribution is reported, not certain.
Sources: Disney, Pinocchio (1940); on-site KJV text of Romans 2:15, Jeremiah 17:9 and 1 Timothy 4:2

Saying: God has a wonderful plan for your life
WhatItMeans: God has a specific, wonderful script written for your life — a good plan, made just for you, that you can step into and enjoy.
WhatTheBibleSays: Jeremiah 29:11 is the verse always quoted for this — "For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the LORD, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end" — but that promise was spoken to the exiles in Babylon as a people, with a seventy-year horizon, not as a personal guarantee of a wonderful life for each believer. God does have purposes for His people — Ephesians 2:10 says we are created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained — yet the Bible never promises the plan will feel wonderful; Paul's own life was shipwrecks, beatings and prison. I believe God has good purposes for every believer, and I also believe the slogan promises more than the verse it leans on.
Origin: Bill Bright, founder of Campus Crusade for Christ (now Cru). He drafted a gospel presentation called "God's Plan for Your Life" in 1956, developed it into the Four Spiritual Laws talking points in 1957, and the booklet form was compiled in 1965, its first law reading: "God loves you and offers a wonderful plan for your life." The booklet went on to be printed in more than 2.5 billion copies in over 200 languages.
RelatedTopics: God's Providence; God's Sovereignty; Guidance; Hope
Sources: Bill Bright, The Four Spiritual Laws (copyright 1965); on-site KJV text of Jeremiah 29:11 and Ephesians 2:10

Saying: The family that prays together stays together
WhatItMeans: A family that prays together will hold together — shared prayer is what keeps a family from falling apart.
WhatTheBibleSays: Prayer together is a good and biblical thing — Jesus said "where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them" (Matthew 18:20), and the early church continued steadfastly in prayer (Acts 2:42). And Joshua's resolve is real: "as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD" (Joshua 24:15). But that verse is about serving the Lord, not about prayer keeping a family together, and the Bible never promises that praying families never break apart. I hold that the slogan points at something true — prayer binds a household to God — while promising something Scripture never does.
Origin: Written in 1947 by advertising copywriter Al Scalpone as the slogan for Fr. Patrick Peyton's Family Rosary Crusade and Family Theater radio dramas. Peyton (1909-1992), the Irish-American Holy Cross priest known as "the Rosary Priest," launched the Family Rosary Crusade in 1942; the slogan was heard weekly on the programme and on billboards.
Sources: Al Scalpone / Fr. Patrick Peyton, Family Rosary Crusade (1947); on-site KJV text of Joshua 24:15, Matthew 18:20 and Acts 2:42

Saying: What goes around comes around
WhatItMeans: Life pays you back in kind — the harm or good you send out will come back to you, sooner or later, as surely as a circle closing.
WhatTheBibleSays: The Bible does teach that actions have consequences: "whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap" (Galatians 6:7), and Proverbs 26:27 says whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein. But the Bible's version is God's justice, not automatic karma — consequences come from the Lord's hand, in His time, and sometimes grace interrupts the circle entirely, as it did for the thief on the cross. I believe the principle behind the saying is biblical, while the saying itself turns God's personal justice into an impersonal law of payback, and that is not the same thing.
Origin: A modern American proverb, first documented in print in 1974 in Eddie Stone's book Donald Writes No More; linguists trace it to an African proverb that entered general use through African-American speech. It was popularised in song — by The Stylistics, and later by Justin Timberlake's 2006 hit. The underlying idea is ancient, but the wording is twentieth-century.
Sources: Eddie Stone, Donald Writes No More (1974); on-site KJV text of Galatians 6:7 and Proverbs 26:27

Saying: The seven deadly sins
WhatItMeans: People take it as a given that the Bible lists seven deadly sins — pride, greed, lust, envy, gluttony, wrath and sloth — a fixed set, named and counted in Scripture.
WhatTheBibleSays: Each of those vices is warned against in Scripture, but the set of seven is not from the Bible at all — it is a church list, shaped by monks and popes centuries after the apostles. The verse people usually mean is Proverbs 6:16-19: "These six things doth the LORD hate: yea, seven are an abomination unto him" — but that list is a proud look, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, a heart that devises wicked imaginations, feet swift in running to mischief, a false witness, and one who sows discord. Only pride appears on both lists. My position is that the seven deadly sins are a useful catalogue of human failure, but they are the church's list, not the Bible's, and the Bible's own seven are mostly outward acts — lying, murder, perjury, sowing division — while the church's seven are mostly inward appetites.
Origin: The list began as eight "evil thoughts" of the desert monk Evagrius Ponticus (c. 346-399), was carried west by John Cassian (c. 360-435) in The Institutes, and was reshaped into seven by Pope Gregory the Great in his Moralia in Job (c. 590): vainglory folded into pride, sadness into acedia (sloth), envy added, pride set as the root. Thomas Aquinas later expounded Gregory's list as the "capital sins" in the Summa Theologica (1265-1274), and the Catechism of the Catholic Church names them in paragraph 1866.
Sources: Evagrius Ponticus; John Cassian, The Institutes; Pope Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job (c. 590); on-site KJV text of Proverbs 6:16-19 and Galatians 5:19-21

Saying: Follow your heart
WhatItMeans: Your heart knows the way — trust your feelings, follow what feels right, and you will end up where you belong.
WhatTheBibleSays: The Bible says the opposite, and bluntly: "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?" (Jeremiah 17:9). Numbers 15:39 warns the people not to seek after their own heart and their own eyes, and Proverbs 3:5 says to trust in the LORD with all thine heart and lean not unto thine own understanding. The verse people sometimes quote for it, Psalm 37:4 — "He shall give thee the desires of thine heart" — only works if you delight yourself in the LORD first. I hold that feelings are real and worth listening to, but the Bible never makes them the guide; a deceitful heart followed faithfully will lead you faithfully astray.
Origin: No single author or first use is known. The idea runs through Romanticism in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and Emerson's Self-Reliance (1841) says "Trust thyself"; the exact phrase appears in literary works and proverbs by the nineteenth century and rises in print from the early twentieth. Its modern ubiquity owes much to Disney — Cinderella (1950), "A Dream Is a Wish Your Heart Makes" — and to Steve Jobs's Stanford commencement address in 2005.
Sources: On-site KJV text of Jeremiah 17:9, Numbers 15:39, Proverbs 3:5 and Psalm 37:4

Saying: Time heals all wounds
WhatItMeans: Given enough time, every hurt fades — grief, betrayal and loss all mend on their own, because time itself does the healing.
WhatTheBibleSays: The Bible names a healer, and it is not time: "He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds" (Psalm 147:3), and "The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart" (Psalm 34:18). Time passes — Ecclesiastes 3:1 says to every thing there is a season — but time on its own has never bound up a wound; people carry old hurts for decades, and some wounds only deepen with the years. I believe the saying is a kind word meant well, but it puts the healing in the calendar instead of in God, and it leaves the grieving person waiting on the clock rather than turning to the Healer.
Origin: The sentiment is ancient — it is traditionally credited to the Greek comic poet Menander (c. 342-290 BC), "time is the healer of all necessary evils," though that attribution is repeated mainly by quotation collections rather than surviving fragments, and some sources credit the poet Diphilus instead. Chaucer has the same thought in Troilus and Criseyde (1380s): "As tyme hem hurt, a tyme doth hem cure." The exact modern wording first appears in print in H. Rider Haggard's novel Morning Star (1910): "Time heals all wounds."
Sources: Chaucer, Troilus and Criseyde (1380s); H. Rider Haggard, Morning Star (1910); on-site KJV text of Psalm 147:3, Psalm 34:18 and Ecclesiastes 3:1
